section: Right to Freedom - Article 19 (six freedoms) and reasonable restrictions
subsections: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner
Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness

accepted.s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the striking down of the ban on the journal *Cross Roads* on the ground that 'public order' was not then a constitutionally recognised restriction on free speech?
o: Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar
Bennett Coleman v Union of India
accepted.x: In Romesh Thappar v State of Madras (1950), the ban on *Cross Roads* was struck down because public order was not then a ground under Article 19(2). The judgment contributed to the First Amendment, 1951.
accepted.tq: Use the case-to-ruling association and distinguish the ruling from other speech cases.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
a. Bennett Coleman v Union of India — Newsprint policy fixing the number of pages violated press freedom
b. Shreya Singhal v Union of India — Section 66A of the Information Technology Act struck down
c. Naveen Jindal case — Flying the national flag recognised as expression under Article 19(1)(a)
d. Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal — Community standards test for obscenity
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
accepted.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Bennett Coleman concerned the newsprint policy, Shreya Singhal concerned Section 66A, Naveen Jindal concerned flying the national flag, and Aveek Sarkar adopted the community standards test for obscenity.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure case-ruling pairs and verify every pair before selecting the code.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: With reference to the freedom of speech and expression, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Bennett Coleman held that the newsprint policy fixing pages did not affect press freedom.
Bennett Coleman applied the community standards test for obscenity.
Bennett Coleman held that the newsprint policy fixing pages violated press freedom.
Bennett Coleman upheld Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
accepted.x: Bennett Coleman v Union of India (1972) held that the newsprint policy fixing the number of pages violated press freedom.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between closely related speech and press cases by identifying the precise subject of the ruling.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down by the Supreme Court in:
o: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar
Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh
Shreya Singhal v Union of India
accepted.x: Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A because it was vague and overbroad.
accepted.tq: Match the statutory provision with the case that invalidated it.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in *Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh* (2023)?
o: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was upheld subject to safeguards.
The grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive and no additional restrictions may be imposed on ministers' speech.
Flying the national flag was held to be outside the protection of Article 19(1)(a).
Public order was held not to be a ground under Article 19(2).
accepted.x: Kaushal Kishor held that the grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive and that no extra restriction can be imposed on ministers' speech. It also recognised that Articles 19 and 21 can be enforced against non-State actors.
accepted.tq: Use the precise holding of the case rather than a broadly related speech-rights proposition.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding important decisions on speech and communication:
1. Kedar Nath Singh upheld sedition only when connected with incitement to violence or public disorder.
2. Anuradha Bhasin recognised speech and trade over the internet as protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).
3. Anuradha Bhasin held that internet shutdowns need not be temporary or proportionate if national security is invoked.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Anuradha Bhasin required shutdowns to be proportionate, temporary and published; therefore, statement 3 is incorrect.
accepted.tq: Find the statement that reverses the safeguards laid down for restrictions on internet access.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The law replacing the Indian Penal Code came into force on:
accepted.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from 1 July 2024.
accepted.tq: Test the exact commencement date against nearby constitutional and legal dates.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding sedition and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is correct?
o: Section 66A BNS replaced sedition and criminal defamation.
Section 152 BNS deals with acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, while sedition as Section 124A IPC is gone.
Sedition was retained in the BNS under Section 356.
Section 124A IPC continues unchanged as Section 124A of the BNS.
accepted.x: Section 124A IPC, which had been kept in abeyance by the Supreme Court in 2022, is gone under the BNS. Section 152 BNS punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.
accepted.tq: Separate the former IPC provision from the new BNS section dealing with sovereignty, unity and integrity.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Criminal defamation, earlier covered by Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code, is now dealt with under which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
accepted.x: Criminal defamation is now covered by Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita; Sections 499 and 500 were the corresponding IPC provisions.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the new BNS section for criminal defamation from sections dealing with other speech-related offences.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is identified with hate speech in the stated legal update?
accepted.x: Hate speech is identified with Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in the stated legal update.
accepted.tq: Link the specific offence to its exact statutory section instead of relying on the familiar IPC numbering.
accepted.sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Under Article 19(2), which one of the following is NOT a ground for imposing a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech and expression?
accepted.x: General public interest is not a ground listed in Article 19(2). Contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence are expressly included.
accepted.tq: Find the ground belonging to another Article 19 clause rather than to Article 19(2).
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is not included among the grounds of restriction under Article 19(2)?
accepted.x: Economic grounds are not included in Article 19(2). Sovereignty and integrity, security of the State and friendly relations with foreign States are among the specified grounds.
accepted.tq: Reject an attractive but constitutionally unlisted ground by checking the exhaustive list.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sedition is expressly listed as a ground under Article 19(2).
2. General public interest is a ground under Article 19(5), but not under Article 19(2).
3. Economic grounds are expressly listed under Article 19(2).
Which of the statements given above is correct?
accepted.x: Only statement 2 is correct. Sedition and economic grounds are not listed in Article 19(2), whereas general public interest is a ground under Article 19(5).
accepted.tq: Split the options by locating each proposed ground in the correct Article 19 clause.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Which of the following grounds are available for restricting freedom of assembly under Article 19(3)?
1. Sovereignty and integrity of India
2. Public order
3. Morality
4. Security of the State
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Article 19(3) permits restrictions on assembly in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India and public order. Morality and security of the State are not listed as grounds in Article 19(3).
accepted.tq: Use the clause-by-clause comparison to avoid importing grounds from Article 19(2) or 19(4).
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: Freedom of association under Article 19(4) may be reasonably restricted in the interests of:
o: Friendly relations with foreign States, public order, and contempt of court
Security of the State, defamation, and public order
Public order, morality, and sovereignty and integrity of India
General public interest, morality, and professional qualifications
accepted.x: Article 19(4) permits restrictions on freedom of association in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, public order and morality.
accepted.tq: Match the freedom with its own restricted set of grounds rather than using the longer speech list.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: A restriction on the freedom to move freely throughout India or to reside and settle in any part of India may be imposed under Article 19(5) in the interests of:
o: Security of the State and friendly relations with foreign States
General public interest and protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
accepted.x: Article 19(5) permits restrictions in the interests of the general public and for protecting the interests of any Scheduled Tribe.
accepted.tq: Identify the correct authority of the restriction by matching movement and residence with Article 19(5).
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground for restricting the freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business under Article 19(6)?
o: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
accepted.x: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes is a ground under Article 19(5), relating to movement and residence. Article 19(6) refers to general public interest, professional or technical qualifications, and State trade or monopoly.
accepted.tq: Spot the ground borrowed from the neighbouring Article 19(5) provision.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article 19 clause)
a. Article 19(2)
b. Article 19(3)
c. Article 19(5)
d. Article 19(6)

List-II (Freedom concerned)
i. Movement and residence
ii. Speech and expression
iii. Profession, trade or business
iv. Assembly
accepted.x: Article 19(2) concerns speech and expression, Article 19(3) assembly, Article 19(5) movement and residence, and Article 19(6) profession, trade or business.
accepted.tq: Start with the familiar clause-freedom pairs and eliminate codes that shift the neighbouring freedoms.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Which of the following grounds were added to Article 19(2) by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Public order
2. Friendly relations with foreign States
3. Incitement to an offence
4. Sovereignty and integrity of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The First Amendment, 1951 added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence to Article 19(2). Sovereignty and integrity of India was added by the Sixteenth Amendment, 1963.
accepted.tq: Separate the grounds added by the First and Sixteenth Amendments instead of treating them as one package.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: The Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963 added which ground to Articles 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4)?
accepted.x: The Sixteenth Amendment, 1963 added sovereignty and integrity of India as a ground in Articles 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4).
accepted.tq: Use the amendment-number and year pair to identify the constitutional ground added across three clauses.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: The State-trade or State-monopoly provision in Article 19(6), which also protects nationalisation, is associated with which Constitutional Amendment?
accepted.x: The First Amendment, 1951 added the State-trade clause in Article 19(6), thereby shielding nationalisation from challenge under the freedom of trade and business.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the amendment associated with State monopoly from the later amendment associated with sovereignty and integrity.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Decision in *Shreya Singhal v Union of India*
B. First Constitutional Amendment adding public order to Article 19(2)
C. Decision in *Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India*
D. Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment adding sovereignty and integrity of India
accepted.x: The correct order is First Amendment (1951), Sixteenth Amendment (1963), Shreya Singhal (2015), and Anuradha Bhasin (2020).
accepted.tq: Fix the amendment years first, then place the two later Supreme Court decisions.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s:
In determining whether a restriction on a fundamental right is reasonable, the court considers which of the following factors?
1. Nature of the right
2. Purpose, extent and urgency of the evil
3. Proportionality
4. Whether the restriction completely eclipses the right itself
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The test of reasonableness includes the nature of the right, the purpose, extent and urgency of the evil, and proportionality. A restriction must not eclipse the right itself.
accepted.tq: Treat the complete test as cumulative and reject any option that omits a stated factor.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: The test for determining the reasonableness of restrictions on fundamental rights is particularly associated with which case?
o: Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
State of Madras v V.G. Row
Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
accepted.x: The reasonableness test, involving factors such as the nature of the right, the purpose and urgency of the restriction, and proportionality, is associated with V.G. Row (1952).
accepted.tq: Identify the case from the constitutional test rather than from a speech-specific statutory ruling.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the scope of reasonable restrictions under Article 19?
o: The existence of a restriction removes the need to examine its purpose and urgency.
Once a restriction is enacted in the public interest, the court cannot examine its reasonableness.
Any restriction connected with economic policy automatically satisfies proportionality.
The court determines reasonableness, and a restriction must not destroy or eclipse the right itself.
accepted.x: The court decides whether a restriction is reasonable by examining factors including purpose, extent, urgency and proportionality. A restriction must not eclipse the fundamental right itself.
accepted.tq: Apply the proportionality principle to distinguish judicial review from unquestioning legislative deference.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: How many heads of reasonable restriction under Article 19 are counted in the India Year Book 2026 reference?
accepted.x: The India Year Book 2026 reference counts 11 heads of reasonable restriction across Article 19.
accepted.tq: Test the exact quantitative total rather than inferring it from the number of Article 19 clauses.
accepted.sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

accepted.s: The year 2026 marks which anniversary of the First Constitutional Amendment?
accepted.x: The year 2026 marks 75 years of the First Constitutional Amendment, which was enacted in 1951.
accepted.tq: Calculate the anniversary from the amendment year while distinguishing it from the amendment's serial number.
